text.p: South Africa, only recently readmitted to the world economy, has started lobbying to play a more prominent regional role in the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.

Finance Department officials on Wednesday said the government wanted its dominance of English-speaking Africa's voting power within the international bodies to be recognised and would bid to host the two groups' annual meeings in 2003.

Deputy director Daniel van Rensburg said that although South Africa's voting power in the IMF ranked 23rd out of 181 member countries, it was not likely to be able to appoint a national as executive director of the African Group One Constituency covering English-speaking Africa for 96 years.

"We only joined the Africa Group One Constituency in October last year, which means that we fall right at the end of the queue," he told told the finance committee of the National Council of Provinces.

"This means that we will only be able to have an executive director in 96 years' time. That is something of concern to South Africa because we are the biggest shareholder in that constituency and...it is an issue that we are discussing with the other members."
South Africa used to be part of the Australian constituency until 1974, when it was forced out because of political pressure, Van Rensburg said.

It was then granted resident representative status in Washington, which was a relatively privileged status as it had direct access to all World Bank and IMF documents even though it could not take part in decision-making.
But now, as part of the English-speaking African group, it fell under its current executive directorship, held by Zimbabwe, and did not have direct access to documents any more.
"We have a huge problem in getting anything back from the IMF and World Bank because our affairs are being held by a constituency," deputy director Johan van Tonder said.

Some members also felt uneasy about the fact that they were now part of a constituency that included Nigeria and said they did not want to be seen to be supporting it because of its human rights problems.
There was some debate about whether South Africa's 13,904 votes, or 0.93 percent of the total votes, gave it any right to try to influence the way the IMF worked.
Some members felt that South Africa was still "small fry" in world terms but Van Rensburg said that it had a higher voting power than countries such as the Netherlands and Poland.
"I think that we should be taken seriously...one of our policies is to influence the decision-making process within these institutions to the benefit of Southern Africa," he said.
Van Rensburg said that South Africa was now gearing up to bid to host the institutions' 2003 annual general meetings after narrowly losing the bid for the 2000 meetings to the Czech Republic.
If successful, this would benefit the South African economy as the meetings would probably be attended by more than 16,000 business people, Van Tonder said.
